summary: Revelation 17 (18 verses) continues the story of lamb and dragon. Starting with 'One of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying, “Come here. I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who sits on man', it moves through themes of lamb and dragon, victory and calls readers toward new creation.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows lamb and dragon lived out in patmos, persecution. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: One of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying, “Come here. I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who sits on many waters,
They are seven kings. Five have fallen, the one is, and the other has not yet come. When he comes, he must continue a little while.
The woman whom you saw is the great city which reigns over the kings of the earth.”

questions.question: What is happening in Revelation 17?
questions.answer: In 18 verses, this chapter revelation 17 (18 verses) continues the story of lamb and dragon. starting with 'one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying, “come here. i will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who sits on man', it moves through themes of lamb and dragon, victory and calls readers toward new creation. The setting is patmos, persecution, written to seven churches in asia. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Revelation and why 17 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally john, addressed to seven churches in asia around ad 90-95. This chapter fits the book's purpose as apocalypse + letters — its themes of lamb and dragon, victory build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'faith' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Trust, loyalty to God. In this chapter, it appears in context of lamb and dragon. For a first-time reader: think of it as trust, loyalty to god, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through lamb and dragon and victory, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 8 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'The beast that you saw was, and is not; and is about to come up out of the abyss and to go into destruction. Those who dwell on the earth and whose names have not been written in t...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about lamb and dragon. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
